card.keepWhy: Head, heart, shoulders. All of you.

sources: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book II (Life of Saint Benedict), chapters 1 and 3: Benedict’s cave at Subiaco; the monks of a nearby monastery (Vicovaro) beg him to be their abbot; he warns them his ways and theirs will not agree; they poison his wine; when the glass is offered to him to bless, as was the custom, he makes the sign of the cross and it breaks as if struck by a stone; he rises calmly, asks God’s mercy on them and returns to his solitude.
Tertullian, De Corona 3 (c. 200, Carthage): Christians trace the sign on the forehead at every going out and coming in, at dressing, at the table, at lighting the lamps, at lying down and sitting.
Matthew 28:19 (baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit).

Catechism of the Catholic Church 1235, 1668 (the sign of the cross and holy water as sacramentals recalling baptism); Western Catholic practice left shoulder then right; Eastern Orthodox right then left.
check: Tertullian’s De Corona is usually dated about 211; the caption says “around the year 200.” Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when something big or scary happens, what does your body do first?
options: that’s so human. this story is about a man who didn’t freeze. listen.
me too, honestly. this one is about reaching for something smaller.
then your hands may already know today’s story. listen.

steps.line: Long ago in Italy, a young man named Benedict left the noisy city behind to pray alone in a mountain cave.
Monks from a nearby monastery begged him to lead them. He warned them his ways were strict. They insisted.
They soon resented his strict rule, so they poisoned his wine. At supper, as the custom was, they handed him the cup to bless.

steps.q: Benedict traces a small cross over the cup, the way he always does. What happens?
steps.why: The cup breaks in his hands. Benedict’s first move was the smallest prayer there is.

steps.line: He made the sign of the cross over it, and the cup shattered, as if a stone had struck it.

steps.q: Benedict knows exactly what they tried to do. What does he do?
o: Has them thrown out of the monastery
Stays, and makes the rule stricter
steps.why: No shouting, no revenge. Gregory the Great, telling it around 593, says Benedict went back to his cave to live alone with himself, before God.

steps.line: He stood up calmly. “God have mercy on you, brothers,” he said. Then he went back to his cave to pray.
The habit was already old. Around the year 200, a writer in North Africa described Christians tracing a little cross on their foreheads all day: dressing, eating, lighting a lamp.
steps.label: history

steps.q: These monks found Benedict too strict. Years later he wrote his own Rule for monks. What is it famous for?
steps.why: In its opening he hopes to set down “nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.” Benedictine, Cistercian and Trappist monks still live by it, fifteen centuries on.

steps.line: Today a pitcher does it before the first throw. A grandmother does it when her bus passes a church. Two seconds: head, heart, shoulders.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Some Catholics also trace three tiny crosses with the thumb: on the forehead, lips and heart. When?
o: Before the first bite of a meal
Just before the Gospel at Mass
When a funeral car passes by
steps.why: Before the Gospel: may the word be in my mind, on my lips, and in my heart.

steps.q: The hand moves head, heart, shoulders while the words are said. Match each place to the words said there.
steps.why: Words and hand keep the same order. The cross is traced over all of you, head, heart and shoulders, with nothing left out.

say: here’s what the hand is saying. it traces the cross, where jesus died, over your whole self. and the words name who catholics believe God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the words jesus gave for baptism at the end of matthew’s gospel.
benedict didn’t panic. he made the smallest prayer and put the moment in God’s hands. western catholics touch the left shoulder first; orthodox christians go right. same sign, two old habits.

steps.q: Many Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door, then make the sign. From this lesson, why put those two together?
o: The water cleans the hand for prayer
It recalls their baptism: water, and those words
It blesses the church as they come in
steps.why: Water, and “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” That’s baptism. At the door, it’s a small reminder of it.

today.say: at your next meal today, before the first bite, you could make the sign slowly, like benedict over his cup. or just pause and notice head, heart, shoulders. your choice.
options: I’ll try it at my next meal
two seconds, and nothing left out. that’s the whole prayer.
that counts. once you start looking, you’ll see it everywhere.
